blocks.text: Read the first and last paragraph, then one line from the middle. Ask: what is the writer doing in the whole passage — explaining, arguing, telling a story, comparing?

head: Option is…
Sign
Verdict
rows: Fits only one paragraph or one example
Covers far more than the passage discusses
Uses the passage's words for a point it never makes
Covers every paragraph and matches the writer's aim

blocks.text: For purpose questions, check the verb: "to warn", "to explain", "to argue". A story passage is rarely "to prove".
A true detail is not the main idea. If it fits only paragraph 2, it is too narrow.

head: Detail (stated)
Inference (supported)
rows: Go back to the exact lines
Join two clues in the text
A small, safe step from the text
Too strong, or true in life only

blocks.text: Always go back to the lines. Never answer a detail question from memory of the passage.
An inference must be provable from the passage. If you need outside knowledge to defend an option, it is wrong.

title: Words in context, tone and structure

items: Words in context: cover the word, read the whole sentence, guess your own word, then pick the option closest to it. Test it by putting it back in the sentence.
Tone: look for judging words (sadly, rightly, merely, remarkable). Most passages are measured: "concerned", "hopeful", "critical", not "furious" or "ecstatic".
Structure: "this", "such", "it" usually point back to the nearest idea before them. Linking words signal the move: however = contrast, therefore = result, for example = support.

blocks.text: The commonest meaning of the word is often a trap. "A grave error" means serious, not a burial place.

head: Trap
What it looks like
Spot it by
rows: Checking the meaning, not the words
Real detail, wrong paragraph or person
Asking: did the writer go that far?
Asking: where does the passage say it?

blocks.text: Cross out wrong options first. With about a minute per question, two quick eliminations often settle it.
Rule: choose the meaning the word has in the given sentence, and keep the same part of speech (verb for verb, adjective for adjective).

items: ✔ "The heavy rain will abate by evening." abate = lessen
✘ abate = increase (the opposite, set as a trap)

blocks.text: Put each option back into the sentence. The one that keeps the meaning unchanged is the answer.
Many words have several meanings: "a sound argument" means valid, not a noise. The sentence decides.
Rule: first find the word's meaning in the sentence, then look for its opposite. One option is usually a synonym planted to catch you.

items: ✔ Opposite of "scarce" (water was scarce) = plentiful
✘ Opposite of "scarce" = rare (a synonym, not the opposite)

blocks.text: Prefixes un-, in-, dis-, im- often make opposites: honest → dishonest, mature → immature.
Not always: "inflammable" means easily set on fire (same as flammable), and "invaluable" means extremely valuable.

items: ✔ Don't lose your ticket.
✘ Don't loose your ticket.

blocks.text: stationEry has E for envelopes; stationAry has A for "at rest".

items: either…or / neither…nor: the verb agrees with the nearer subject.
each, every, everyone, either, neither (alone): singular verb.
A number of students are… (plural) · The number of students is… (singular).
as well as, along with, together with do not change the subject: The captain, along with his players, is here.
If + present → will: If it rains, we will stay.
If + past → would: If I had time, I would help.
If + had done → would have done: If he had studied, he would have passed.
✔ Neither the teacher nor the students were late.
✘ Neither the teacher nor the students was late.

blocks.text: Never put "will" or "would" in the if-part: ✘ If it will rain…

items: a / an goes by sound: an hour, an honest man, a university, a European.
the: something already mentioned, one of a kind (the sun), and superlatives (the best).
✔ This phone is superior to that one.
✘ This phone is superior than that one.

blocks.text: superior, inferior, senior and junior take "to", never "than". Prefer X to Y, never "prefer X than Y"; with verbs: prefer to do X rather than (do) Y.

head: Rule
✘ Wrong
✔ Right
rows: Walking to school, the rain started.
Walking to school, I was caught in the rain.
She likes swimming, reading and to cook.
She likes swimming, reading and cooking.

blocks.text: Pronoun test: drop the other person. "Ali came with me" is clearly right, so "with Sara and me", not "with Sara and I".
